claim: Adapting to the environment statistics by reducing brain responses to repetitive sensory information is key for efficient information processing.
source: Adapting to the environment statistics by reducing brain responses to repetitive sensory information is key for efficient information processing.
evidence: This is a general statement about adaptive processing supported by established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The fine-scale computations that support adaptive processing in the human brain remain largely unknown.
source: Yet, the fine-scale computations that support this adaptive processing in the human brain remain largely unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge about adaptive processing mechanisms.

claim: Ultra-high field imaging affords sub-millimetre resolution necessary to examine fMRI signals across cortical depth in a non-invasive manner.
source: Ultra-high field (UHF) imaging affords the sub-millimetre resolution necessary to examine fMRI signals across cortical depth in a non-invasive manner, providing a unique approach to interrogate human brain circuits at a finer scale (for review: Lawrence et al., 2019a) than that possible by standard fMRI techniques (for review: Goense et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles discussing UHF imaging capabilities.

claim: Sensory inputs enter the cortex from the thalamus at the level of the middle layer (layer 4).
source: In particular, sensory inputs are known to enter the cortex from the thalamus at the level of the middle layer (layer 4), while output information is fed forward from superficial layers (layer 2/3), and feedback information is exchanged primarily between deeper layers (layer 5/6) as well as superficial layers (for review: Self et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on laminar circuits.

claim: Output information is fed forward from superficial layers (layer 2/3).
source: In particular, sensory inputs are known to enter the cortex from the thalamus at the level of the middle layer (layer 4), while output information is fed forward from superficial layers (layer 2/3), and feedback information is exchanged primarily between deeper layers (layer 5/6) as well as superficial layers (for review: Self et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on laminar circuits.

claim: Feedback information is exchanged primarily between deeper layers (layer 5/6) as well as superficial layers.
source: In particular, sensory inputs are known to enter the cortex from the thalamus at the level of the middle layer (layer 4), while output information is fed forward from superficial layers (layer 2/3), and feedback information is exchanged primarily between deeper layers (layer 5/6) as well as superficial layers (for review: Self et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on laminar circuits.

claim: Adaptation alters orientation-specific signals across cortical depth in the visual cortex with stronger fMRI-adaptation in superficial layers.
source: We demonstrate that adaptation alters orientation-specific signals across cortical depth in the visual cortex with stronger fMRI-adaptation (i.e. BOLD decrease for repeated stimuli) in superficial layers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Layer-specific fMRI adaptation relates to a perceptual bias in orientation discrimination due to adaptation.
source: This layer-specific fMRI adaptation relates to a perceptual bias in orientation discrimination due to adaptation, as measured using a tilt aftereffect paradigm (e.g. Gibson and Radner, 1937).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a behavioral experiment and a citation to previous work on tilt aftereffect.

claim: Adaptation involves enhanced feedforward connectivity between V1 superficial layers and middle layers of extrastriate visual areas.
source: Further, functional connectivity analysis shows that adaptation involves: (a) enhanced feedforward connectivity between V1 superficial layers and middle layers of extrastriate visual areas, and (b) enhanced short-range feedback between V2 and V1 deeper cortical layers.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on functional connectivity analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Adaptation involves enhanced short-range feedback between V2 and V1 deeper cortical layers.
source: Further, functional connectivity analysis shows that adaptation involves: (a) enhanced feedforward connectivity between V1 superficial layers and middle layers of extrastriate visual areas, and (b) enhanced short-range feedback between V2 and V1 deeper cortical layers.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on functional connectivity analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There is enhanced feedback connectivity from posterior parietal cortex to V1 deeper layers during adaptation.
source: Our results show enhanced feedback connectivity from posterior parietal cortex to V1 deeper layers, suggesting top-down influences on visual processing via long-range feedback mechanisms.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on functional connectivity analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The brain reduces its responses to repeatedly or continuously presented sensory inputs.
source: The brain is known to address this challenge by reducing its responses to repeatedly or continuously presented sensory inputs (for reviews: Clifford, 2002; Kohn, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on sensory adaptation.

claim: Sensory adaptation is a rapid form of plasticity that is critical for efficient processing.
source: This type of sensory adaptation is a rapid form of plasticity that is critical for efficient processing and has been shown to involve changes in perceptual sensitivity (for review: Clifford, 2002) and neural selectivity (for review: Kohn, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on sensory adaptation.

claim: Sensory adaptation involves changes in perceptual sensitivity.
source: This type of sensory adaptation is a rapid form of plasticity that is critical for efficient processing and has been shown to involve changes in perceptual sensitivity (for review: Clifford, 2002) and neural selectivity (for review: Kohn, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Sensory adaptation involves changes in neural selectivity.
source: This type of sensory adaptation is a rapid form of plasticity that is critical for efficient processing and has been shown to involve changes in perceptual sensitivity (for review: Clifford, 2002) and neural selectivity (for review: Kohn, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Neurophysiological studies have shown sensory adaptation to be associated with reduction in neuronal responses that are specific to the features of the adaptor.
source: Numerous neurophysiological studies (for review: Kohn, 2007) have shown sensory adaptation to be associated with reduction in neuronal responses that are specific to the features of the adaptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on neurophysiological studies.

claim: Functional brain imaging studies in humans have shown fMRI adaptation for low-level visual features as indicated by decreased BOLD responses in visual cortex due to stimulus repetition.
source: Functional brain imaging studies in humans have shown f﻿unctional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) adaptation for low-level visual features (e.g. contrast, orientation, motion; for review Larsson et al., 2016) as indicated by decreased BOLD responses in visual cortex due to stimulus repetition.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on fMRI adaptation.

claim: Similar BOLD decreases have been reported in higher visual areas for repeated presentation of more complex visual stimuli, an effect known as repetition suppression.
source: Similar BOLD decreases have been reported in higher visual areas for repeated presentation of more complex visual stimuli (e.g. faces objects), an effect known as repetition suppression (Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Krekelberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on repetition suppression.

claim: Neurophysiological studies provide evidence of rapid adaptation at early stages of sensory processing in primary visual cortex.
source: In particular, neurophysiological studies focussing on primary visual cortex provide evidence of rapid adaptation at early stages of sensory processing (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008; Whitmire and Stanley, 2016; Xiang and Brown, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: fMRI studies have suggested top-down influences on sensory processing of repeated stimuli via feedback mechanisms.
source: In contrast, fMRI studies have suggested top-down influences on sensory processing of repeated stimuli via feedback mechanisms (e.g. Ewbank et al., 2011; Summerfield et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI at standard resolution does not allow us to discern feedforward from feedback signals.
source: Yet, the circuit mechanisms that mediate adaptive processing in the human brain remain largely unknown, as fMRI at standard resolution does not allow us to discern feedforward from feedback signals.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about the limitations of standard fMRI resolution.

claim: There was a significant main effect of ROI (V1, V2, V3, V4) on fMRI responses (F(3,39)=23.276, p=0.001).
source: In particular, a repeated measures ANOVA showed significant main effects of ROI (V1, V2, V3, V4; F(3,39)=23.276, p=0.001), cortical depth (deeper, middle, superficial; F(2,26)=4.942, p=0.034), and condition (adaptation non-adaptation; F(1,13)=11.872, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: There was a significant main effect of cortical depth on fMRI responses (F(2,26)=4.942, p=0.034).
source: In particular, a repeated measures ANOVA showed significant main effects of ROI (V1, V2, V3, V4; F(3,39)=23.276, p=0.001), cortical depth (deeper, middle, superficial; F(2,26)=4.942, p=0.034), and condition (adaptation non-adaptation; F(1,13)=11.872, p=0.004).

claim: There was a significant main effect of condition (adaptation vs. non-adaptation) on fMRI responses (F(1,13)=11.872, p=0.004).

claim: There was no significant ROI × condition × cortical depth interaction (F(6,78)=1.949, p=0.131), suggesting similar fMRI adaptation across visual areas.
source: There was no significant ROI × condition × cortical depth interaction (F(6,78)=1.949, p=0.131), suggesting similar fMRI adaptation across visual areas.

claim: A significant condition × cortical depth interaction (F(2,26)=9.506, p=0.002) indicated stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial and middle than deeper layers.
source: A significant condition × cortical depth interaction (F(2,26)=9.506, p=0.002) indicated stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial and middle than deeper layers.

claim: Following spatial regression analysis correction, there was stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial layers across visual areas, as indicated by a significant condition × cortical depth interaction (F(2,26)=5.996, p=0.022).
source: We observed stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial layers across visual areas following this correction (Figure 3A), as indicated by a significant condition × cortical depth interaction: F(2,26)=5.996, p=0.022.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis after applying a correction method.

source: Post-hoc comparisons showed significantly stronger fMRI adaptation across visual areas in superficial compared to deeper layers (V1: t(14)=−2.556, p=0.023; V3: t(14)=−2.580, p=0.022; V4: t(13)=−2.091, p=0.012; with the exception of V2: t(14)=−0.881, p=0.393)

source: No significant differences were observed between fMRI adaptation in superficial and middle cortical layers across visual areas (V1: t(14)=−2.093, p=0.055; V2: t(14)=0.331, p=0.746; V3: t(14)=0.942, p=0.362; V4: t(13)=−2.096, p=0.056).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of the experimental data.

claim: BOLD measured by GE-EPI is higher at the cortical surface due to vascular contributions.
source: First, it is known that BOLD measured by GE-EPI is higher at the cortical surface due to vascular contributions (Uğurbil et al., 2003; Uludağ et al., 2009; Yacoub et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on BOLD imaging.

claim: Following superficial bias corrections, the superficial bias in the GE-EPI acquired BOLD was significantly reduced.
source: Figure 2F shows that following these corrections the superficial bias in the GE-EPI acquired BOLD was significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a result from the control analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The superficial bias corrections resulted in a significant interaction between GE-EPI acquired BOLD signal from different cortical depths before vs. after correction (F(2,28)=58.556, p<0.0001).
source: That is, the magnitude and variance of GE-EPI BOLD signals from voxels closer to the pial surface were reduced, as indicated by a significant interaction between GE-EPI acquired BOLD signal from different cortical depths (deeper, middle, superficial) before vs. after correction (F(2,28)=58.556, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis.

claim: 3D GRASE sequence is sensitive to signals from small vessels and less affected by larger veins, resulting in higher spatial specificity of the measured BOLD signal.
source: Second, we scanned a subset of participants (N = 5) with a 3D GRASE sequence that is known to be sensitive to signals from small vessels and less affected by larger veins, resulting in higher spatial specificity of the measured BOLD signal (e.g. De Martino et al., 2013; Kemper et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on 3D GRASE imaging.

claim: The 3D GRASE data showed overall lower BOLD signal in V1 compared to the GE-EPI acquired BOLD data.
source: Consistent with previous studies (De Martino et al., 2013), the 3D GRASE data showed: (a) overall lower BOLD signal in V1 compared to the GE-EPI acquired BOLD data and (b) similar BOLD amplitude across V1 cortical depths.
evidence: This is a result from the control experiment with 3D GRASE imaging, supported by a citation.

claim: The 3D GRASE data showed similar BOLD amplitude across V1 cortical depths.
source: Consistent with previous studies (De Martino et al., 2013), the 3D GRASE data showed: (a) overall lower BOLD signal in V1 compared to the GE-EPI acquired BOLD data and (b) similar BOLD amplitude across V1 cortical depths.
evidence: This is a result from the control experiment with 3D GRASE imaging, supported by a citation.

claim: There were no significant differences in BOLD acquired with 3D GRASE vs. the corrected GE-EPI BOLD signal across cortical depths (F(2,6)=2.878, p=0.187).
source: In particular there were no significant differences in BOLD acquired with 3D GRASE vs. the corrected GE-EPI BOLD signal across cortical depths (i.e. no significant sequence × cortical depth interaction: F(2,6)=2.878, p=0.187), suggesting that our superficial bias corrections reduced substantially the contribution of vasculature-related signals in GE-EPI measurements.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis comparing two imaging sequences.

claim: The mean performance on the RSVP task across participants did not differ significantly between adaptation and non-adaptation conditions (t(12)=0.312, p=0.76).
source: In particular, the mean performance across participants (adaptation condition: 62.7 ± 0.3%; non-adaptation condition 60.15 ± 0.4%, SEM) did not differ significantly between conditions (t(12)=0.312, p=0.76).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data during scanning.

claim: Correlating perceptual adaptation index and fMRI adaptation showed a significant correlation for superficial layers (r = 0.656, p=0.039).
source: Correlating a perceptual adaptation index (i.e. difference in the perceived orientation of a test grating between adaptation and non-adaptation conditions) and fMRI adaptation (i.e. mean fMRI adaptation index across V1, V2, V3, and V4) showed a significant correlation for superficial (r = 0.656, p=0.039) but not middle (r = 0.562, p=0.091), nor deeper (r = 0.567, p=0.087) layers.
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlating behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: Correlating perceptual adaptation index and fMRI adaptation showed no significant correlation for middle layers (r = 0.562, p=0.091).
source: Correlating a perceptual adaptation index (i.e. difference in the perceived orientation of a test grating between adaptation and non-adaptation conditions) and fMRI adaptation (i.e. mean fMRI adaptation index across V1, V2, V3, and V4) showed a significant correlation for superficial (r = 0.656, p=0.039) but not middle (r = 0.562, p=0.091), nor deeper (r = 0.567, p=0.087) layers.
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlating behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: Correlating perceptual adaptation index and fMRI adaptation showed no significant correlation for deeper layers (r = 0.567, p=0.087).
source: Correlating a perceptual adaptation index (i.e. difference in the perceived orientation of a test grating between adaptation and non-adaptation conditions) and fMRI adaptation (i.e. mean fMRI adaptation index across V1, V2, V3, and V4) showed a significant correlation for superficial (r = 0.656, p=0.039) but not middle (r = 0.562, p=0.091), nor deeper (r = 0.567, p=0.087) layers.
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlating behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: Laminar-specific fMRI adaptation in visual cortex relates to perceptual bias in orientation discrimination due to adaptation.
source: These results suggest that laminar-specific fMRI adaptation in visual cortex relates to perceptual bias in orientation discrimination due to adaptation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the correlation analysis between behavioral and fMRI data.

claim: Posterior parietal cortex regions (IPS1, IPS2) are involved in processing expectation due to stimulus familiarity.
source: We next tested for adaptive processing in posterior parietal cortex regions (IPS1 IPS2; Benson et al., 2014; Benson et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2015) that have been shown to be involved in processing expectation due to stimulus familiarity (de Lange et al., 2018; Garrido et al., 2009; Li et al., 2010; Summerfield and de Lange, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on posterior parietal cortex function.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of condition in IPS regions (F(1,14)=7.994, p=0.013).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA (ROI [IPS1 IPS2], condition [adaptation non-adaptation], and cortical depth [deeper, middle, superficial]) showed a significant main effect of condition (i.e. decreased fMRI responses for adaptation compared to non-adaptation [F(1,14)=7.994, p=0.013]) and cortical depth (F(2,28)=25.824, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of IPS regions.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant main effect of cortical depth in IPS regions (F(2,28)=25.824, p<0.0001).
source: A repeated measures ANOVA (ROI [IPS1 IPS2], condition [adaptation non-adaptation], and cortical depth [deeper, middle, superficial]) showed a significant main effect of condition (i.e. decreased fMRI responses for adaptation compared to non-adaptation [F(1,14)=7.994, p=0.013]) and cortical depth (F(2,28)=25.824, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of IPS regions.

claim: There were no significant interactions between condition and cortical depth in IPS regions (F(2,28)=0.575, p=0.511).
source: We did not observe any significant interactions between condition and cortical depth (F(2,28)=0.575, p=0.511), nor between ROI, condition, and cortical depth (F(2,28)=0.639, p=0.510), suggesting similar fMRI adaptation effects across cortical layers (Figure 4), rather than layer-specific fMRI adaptation, in posterior parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of IPS regions with an interpretation.

claim: There were no significant interactions between ROI, condition, and cortical depth in IPS regions (F(2,28)=0.639, p=0.510).
source: We did not observe any significant interactions between condition and cortical depth (F(2,28)=0.575, p=0.511), nor between ROI, condition, and cortical depth (F(2,28)=0.639, p=0.510), suggesting similar fMRI adaptation effects across cortical layers (Figure 4), rather than layer-specific fMRI adaptation, in posterior parietal cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data analysis of IPS regions with an interpretation.

claim: Anatomical connections between superficial V1 layers and middle layers of higher areas relate to feedforward processing.
source: UHF fMRI allows us to interrogate the finer functional connectivity across areas based on known anatomical models of connectivity across cortical layers. Recent work (for review: Lawrence et al., 2019a) has proposed that anatomical connections between superficial V1 layers and middle layers of higher areas relate to feedforward processing, while anatomical connections between deeper V1 layers and deeper layers of higher areas relate to feedback processing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on laminar connectivity.

claim: Anatomical connections between deeper V1 layers and deeper layers of higher areas relate to feedback processing.
source: UHF fMRI allows us to interrogate the finer functional connectivity across areas based on known anatomical models of connectivity across cortical layers. Recent work (for review: Lawrence et al., 2019a) has proposed that anatomical connections between superficial V1 layers and middle layers of higher areas relate to feedforward processing, while anatomical connections between deeper V1 layers and deeper layers of higher areas relate to feedback processing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on laminar connectivity.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant three-way interaction between connections, pathways, and condition (F(4,52)=3.574, p=0.027).
source: In particular, a repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant three-way interaction (F(4,52)=3.574, p=0.027) between connections (V1–V2, V1–V3, V1–V4, V1–IPS1, V1–IPS2), pathways (feedforward feedback), and condition (adaptation non-adaptation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant pathway × connection interaction (F(4,52)=3.945, p=0.022).
source: Further, we tested whether the difference in connectivity between adaptation and non-adaptation (i.e. difference in Fisher z-transformed values) differed between pathways (feedforward feedback) and across connections (V1–V2, V1–V3, V1–V4, V1–IPS1, V1–IPS2). A repeated measures ANOVA showed a significant pathway (feedforward feedback) × connection (V1–V2, V1–V3, V1–V4, V1–IPS1, V1–IPS2) interaction (F(4,52)=3.945, p=0.022).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis.

claim: Post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and V2 middle layers for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(14)=2.324, p=0.036).
source: For functional connectivity within visual cortex, post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and middle layers of higher visual areas for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (V1–V2: t(14)=2.324, p=0.036; V1–V3: t(14)=2.778, p=0.016; V1–V4: t(13)=2.778, p=0.0157), suggesting enhanced feedforward processing for adaptation within visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data.

claim: Post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and V3 middle layers for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(14)=2.778, p=0.016).
source: For functional connectivity within visual cortex, post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and middle layers of higher visual areas for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (V1–V2: t(14)=2.324, p=0.036; V1–V3: t(14)=2.778, p=0.016; V1–V4: t(13)=2.778, p=0.0157), suggesting enhanced feedforward processing for adaptation within visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data.

claim: Post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and V4 middle layers for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(13)=2.778, p=0.0157).
source: For functional connectivity within visual cortex, post-hoc comparisons showed significantly higher connectivity between V1 superficial and middle layers of higher visual areas for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (V1–V2: t(14)=2.324, p=0.036; V1–V3: t(14)=2.778, p=0.016; V1–V4: t(13)=2.778, p=0.0157), suggesting enhanced feedforward processing for adaptation within visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data.

claim: No significant differences between conditions were observed in functional connectivity between V1 and V3 deeper layers (t(14)=0.703, p=0.494).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed in functional connectivity between deeper layers in V1 and higher visual areas (V3: t(14)=0.703, p=0.494; V4: t(13)=0.813, p=0.431) with the exception of V1–V2 connectivity (t(14)=2.223, p=0.043), suggesting enhanced short-range feedback connectivity between V2 and V1 deeper layers for adaptation.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data.

claim: No significant differences between conditions were observed in functional connectivity between V1 and V4 deeper layers (t(13)=0.813, p=0.431).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed in functional connectivity between deeper layers in V1 and higher visual areas (V3: t(14)=0.703, p=0.494; V4: t(13)=0.813, p=0.431) with the exception of V1–V2 connectivity (t(14)=2.223, p=0.043), suggesting enhanced short-range feedback connectivity between V2 and V1 deeper layers for adaptation.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data.

claim: There was significantly higher connectivity between V1 and V2 deeper layers for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(14)=2.223, p=0.043).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed in functional connectivity between deeper layers in V1 and higher visual areas (V3: t(14)=0.703, p=0.494; V4: t(13)=0.813, p=0.431) with the exception of V1–V2 connectivity (t(14)=2.223, p=0.043), suggesting enhanced short-range feedback connectivity between V2 and V1 deeper layers for adaptation.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post-hoc comparisons of functional connectivity data with an interpretation.

claim: There was significantly higher functional connectivity between V1 deeper layers and IPS1 for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(14)=3.014, p=0.009).
source: Our results showed significantly higher functional connectivity between V1 deeper layers and IPS1 for adaptation compared to the non-adaptation (t(14)=3.014, p=0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis.

claim: There was fMRI adaptation in V1 deeper layers (t(14)=3.438, p=0.004).
source: This result is consistent with fMRI adaptation in V1 deeper layers (t(14)=3.438, p=0.004) and suggests enhanced feedback processing for visual adaptation.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI data analysis with an interpretation.

claim: No significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between V1 superficial layers and IPS1 (t(14)=1.242, p=0.235).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between: (a) V1 superficial layers and IPS1 (i.e. functional connectivity related to feedforward processing) (t(14)=1.242, p=0.235), (b) V1 and IPS2 (V1 deeper layers and IPS2: t(14)=1. 243, p=0.234; V1 superficial layers and IPS2: t(14)=0.629, p=0.539), and (c) extrastriate visual areas and IPS regions (all p>0.146), suggesting specificity of feedback connectivity for adaptation between V1 and IPS1.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis with an interpretation.

claim: No significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between V1 deeper layers and IPS2 (t(14)=1.243, p=0.234).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between: (a) V1 superficial layers and IPS1 (i.e. functional connectivity related to feedforward processing) (t(14)=1.242, p=0.235), (b) V1 and IPS2 (V1 deeper layers and IPS2: t(14)=1. 243, p=0.234; V1 superficial layers and IPS2: t(14)=0.629, p=0.539), and (c) extrastriate visual areas and IPS regions (all p>0.146), suggesting specificity of feedback connectivity for adaptation between V1 and IPS1.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis with an interpretation.

claim: No significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between V1 superficial layers and IPS2 (t(14)=0.629, p=0.539).
source: In contrast, no significant differences between conditions were observed for functional connectivity between: (a) V1 superficial layers and IPS1 (i.e. functional connectivity related to feedforward processing) (t(14)=1.242, p=0.235), (b) V1 and IPS2 (V1 deeper layers and IPS2: t(14)=1. 243, p=0.234; V1 superficial layers and IPS2: t(14)=0.629, p=0.539), and (c) extrastriate visual areas and IPS regions (all p>0.146), suggesting specificity of feedback connectivity for adaptation between V1 and IPS1.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the functional connectivity analysis with an interpretation.

claim: A regression analysis showed a significant relationship (r = 0.715, p=0.003) between fMRI adaptation in deeper layers of V1 and deeper layers of IPS1.
source: Further, a regression analysis showed a significant relationship (r = 0.715, p=0.003) between fMRI adaptation (i.e. difference in z-scored BOLD between adaptation and non-adaptation) in deeper layers of V1 and deeper layers of IPS1.
evidence: This is a statistical result from a regression analysis.

claim: fMRI adaptation in deeper layers of IPS1 predicts fMRI adaptation in deeper layers of V1.
source: These results suggest that fMRI adaptation in deeper layers of IPS1 predicts fMRI adaptation in deeper layers of V1, consistent with enhanced feedback occipito-parietal connectivity for adaptive processing (i.e. top-down influences from IPS1 to processing of visual information in deeper V1 layers).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the regression analysis result.

claim: hMT+ is anatomically connected to V1.
source: Finally, to test whether our results were specific to functional connectivity within the visual cortex and between V1 and IPS, we tested connectivity with hMT+ as a control region that is known to be anatomically connected to V1 (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991) but its function relates to motion rather than orientation processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an anatomical study.

claim: hMT+ function relates to motion rather than orientation processing.
source: Finally, to test whether our results were specific to functional connectivity within the visual cortex and between V1 and IPS, we tested connectivity with hMT+ as a control region that is known to be anatomically connected to V1 (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991) but its function relates to motion rather than orientation processing.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hMT+ function.

claim: Analysing BOLD responses across cortical depths in hMT+ did not show significant fMRI adaptation.
source: Analysing BOLD responses across cortical depths did not show significant fMRI adaptation. A repeated measures ANOVA did not show a significant main effect of condition (F(1,14)=3.874, p=0.069), cortical depth (F(2,28)=2.898, p=0.101), nor a significant cortical depth × condition interaction (F(2,28)=2.392, p=0.138).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis with hMT+.

claim: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA did not show any significant differences in functional connectivity pathways between V1 and hMT+ across conditions (F(1,14)=0.475, p=0.502).
source: A two-way repeated measures ANOVA did not show any significant differences in these functional connectivity pathways between conditions (i.e. no significant pathway × condition interaction: F(1,14)=0.475, p=0.502).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control analysis with hMT+.

claim: Changes in functional connectivity due to adaptation are specific to connectivity within visual cortex and between V1 and IPS.
source: These results suggest that changes in functional connectivity due to adaptation are specific to connectivity within visual cortex (early and extrastriate areas) and between V1 and IPS.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the control analysis with hMT+.

claim: Visual adaptation involves recurrent processing of orientation information in visual cortex.
source: Our results demonstrate that visual adaptation involves recurrent processing of orientation information in visual cortex, as indicated by orientation-specific fMRI adaptation (i.e. BOLD decreases due to stimulus repetition) across cortical depths with stronger effects in superficial and middle than deeper layers.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the main findings.

claim: The findings are consistent with a recent study showing stronger fMRI responses in superficial V1 layers for visual adaptation in the context of the Flash Grab aftereffect.
source: Our findings are consistent with a recent study (Ge et al., 2020) showing stronger fMRI responses in superficial V1 layers for visual adaptation in the context of the Flash Grab aftereffect.
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to a previous study via citation.

claim: Horizontal connections across V1 columns mediate iso-orientation inhibition.
source: Horizontal connections across V1 columns are known to mediate iso-orientation inhibition (Malach et al., 1993) that is suppression of neurons that are selective for the same orientation across columns.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on V1 horizontal connections.

claim: Iso-orientation inhibition is more pronounced in superficial layers and supports orientation tuning.
source: Iso-orientation inhibition is shown to be more pronounced in superficial layers and support orientation tuning (Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on iso-orientation inhibition.

claim: Horizontal connections between V1 columns primarily terminate in middle and superficial layers.
source: In particular, previous work has shown that horizontal connections between V1 columns primarily terminate in middle and superficial layers (Rockland and Pandya, 1979) and pyramidal cells in superficial layers make extensive arborisations within the same layer (Douglas and Martin, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on V1 anatomy.

claim: Pyramidal cells in superficial layers make extensive arborisations within the same layer.
source: In particular, previous work has shown that horizontal connections between V1 columns primarily terminate in middle and superficial layers (Rockland and Pandya, 1979) and pyramidal cells in superficial layers make extensive arborisations within the same layer (Douglas and Martin, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on pyramidal cell anatomy.

claim: Previous neurophysiological studies have shown stronger decrease in neural population responses due to stimulus repetition in superficial layers of V1, while delayed adaptation effects in middle and deeper levels.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, previous neurophysiological studies have shown stronger decrease in neural population responses due to stimulus repetition in superficial layers of V1, while delayed adaptation effects in middle and deeper levels (Westerberg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a neurophysiological study.

claim: Synaptic input to superficial layers may result due to increase in feedback signals carried by neurons that have dendrites projecting to the superficial layers and their cell bodies in deeper layers.
source: Previous work has shown that synaptic input to superficial layers may result due to increase in feedback signals carried by neurons that have dendrites projecting to the superficial layers and their cell bodies in deeper layers (Larkum, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on synaptic input.

claim: Summerfield et al., 2008 showed stronger repetition suppression in the lateral occipito-temporal cortex for identical stimulus pairs that were repeated frequently.
source: In particular, Summerfield et al., 2008 showed stronger repetition suppression in the lateral occipito-temporal cortex for identical stimulus pairs that were repeated frequently, providing evidence for a role of top-down influences (i.e. expectation) in repetition suppression and visual processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on repetition suppression.

claim: According to predictive coding theory, perception results from comparing feedback expectation and prediction signals in upstream regions with feedforward signals in sensory areas.
source: According to this framework, perception results from comparing feedback expectation and prediction signals in upstream regions with feedforward signals in sensory areas.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: When prediction signals match with sensory input, the error is low; when the expectation does not match with the sensory input, the prediction error is high resulting in increased neural responses for unexpected compared to expected stimuli.
source: When these signals match, the error (i.e. the difference between the prediction fed back and the incoming sensory input) is low; in contrast, when the expectation does not match with the sensory input, the prediction error is high resulting in increased neural responses for unexpected compared to expected (i.e. repeated stimuli).
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory principles.

claim: Bastos et al., 2012 have proposed a microcircuit model of predictive coding that combines excitatory and inhibitory properties of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers.
source: Bastos et al., 2012 have proposed a microcircuit model of predictive coding that combines excitatory and inhibitory properties of pyramidal neurons across cortical layers to account for prediction encoding, prediction errors, and modulation of incoming sensory inputs to minimise prediction error.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a theoretical model.

claim: GE-EPI remains limited by vasculature-related signals contributing to BOLD at the cortical surface, resulting in loss of spatial specificity.
source: It is important to note that despite the advances afforded by UHF imaging, GE-EPI remains limited by vasculature-related signals contributing to BOLD at the cortical surface, resulting in loss of spatial specificity (Kay et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation discussing limitations of GE-EPI.

claim: The findings on orientation-specific adaptation in superficial layers are consistent with previous laminar imaging studies showing BOLD effects in superficial layers in a range of tasks.
source: Our findings on orientation-specific adaptation in superficial layers are consistent with previous laminar imaging studies showing BOLD effects in superficial layers in a range of tasks (De Martino et al., 2015; Olman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings to previous studies via citations.

claim: Recent advances in cerebral blood volume imaging using vascular space occupancy could be exploited in future studies to enhance the spatial specificity of laminar imaging in the human brain.
source: Recent advances in cerebral blood volume (CBV) imaging using vascular space occupancy (VASO) (e.g. Beckett et al., 2020; Huber et al., 2019) could be exploited in future studies to enhance the spatial specificity of laminar imaging in the human brain.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations to recent methodological advances.

claim: Adaptive processing in the human brain engages a circuit that integrates recurrent processing within visual cortex with top-down influences from posterior parietal cortex via feedback.
source: In sum, exploiting UHF imaging, we provide evidence that adaptive processing in the human brain engages a circuit that integrates recurrent processing within visual cortex with top-down influences (i.e. stimulus expectation) from posterior parietal cortex via feedback.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: This circuit of local recurrent and feedback influences is critical for rapid brain plasticity that supports efficient sensory processing by suppressing familiar and expected information to facilitate resource allocation to new incoming input.
source: This circuit of local recurrent and feedback influences is critical for rapid brain plasticity that supports efficient sensory processing by suppressing familiar and expected information to facilitate resource allocation to new incoming input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Gamma oscillations are linked to feedforward processing in input layers.
source: Combining laminar imaging with electrophysiological recordings has the potential to shed more light on the dynamics of this circuit, consistent with recent evidence (Buffalo et al., 2011; Self et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014) that gamma oscillations are linked to feedforward processing in input layers, while alpha/beta oscillations are related to feedback mechanisms in superficial and deeper cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Alpha/beta oscillations are related to feedback mechanisms in superficial and deeper cortical layers.
source: Combining laminar imaging with electrophysiological recordings has the potential to shed more light on the dynamics of this circuit, consistent with recent evidence (Buffalo et al., 2011; Self et al., 2013; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014) that gamma oscillations are linked to feedforward processing in input layers, while alpha/beta oscillations are related to feedback mechanisms in superficial and deeper cortical layers.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: Eighteen healthy volunteers (11 females and 7 males) participated in the study.
source: Eighteen healthy volunteers (11 females and 7 males) participated in the study.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Data from two participants were excluded from further analysis due to excessive head movement (higher than 1.5 mm) and technical problems during acquisition.
source: Data from two participants were excluded from further analysis due to excessive head movement (higher than 1.5 mm) and technical problems during acquisition, resulting in data from 15 participants for the main experiment (mean age: 24.44 years and SD: 3.83 years).
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria and final sample size.

claim: The final sample for the main experiment consisted of 15 participants with mean age 24.44 years and SD 3.83 years.
source: Data from two participants were excluded from further analysis due to excessive head movement (higher than 1.5 mm) and technical problems during acquisition, resulting in data from 15 participants for the main experiment (mean age: 24.44 years and SD: 3.83 years).
evidence: This describes the final sample characteristics.

claim: Five participants were scanned with a 3D GRASE EPI sequence.
source: Five participants (four who participated in the main experiment and an additional participant) were scanned with a 3D GRASE EPI sequence.
evidence: This describes the control experiment sample.

claim: Twelve of the participants who took part in the fMRI experiment completed an additional psychophysical experiment.
source: Twelve of the participants who took part in the fMRI experiment completed an additional psychophysical experiment.
evidence: This describes the behavioral experiment sample.

claim: The study was approved by the local Ethical Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Neuroscience at Maastricht University and the University of Cambridge Ethics Committee (ethics number PRE2017.057).
source: The study was approved by the local Ethical Committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Neuroscience at Maastricht University and the University of Cambridge Ethics Committee (ethics number PRE2017.057).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Stimuli comprised sinewave gratings (one cycle per degree) of varying orientations.
source: Stimuli comprised sinewave gratings (one cycle per degree) of varying orientations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: The equi-volume approach has been shown to reduce misclassification of voxels to layers, in particular for ROIs presenting high curvature.
source: Following previous studies, we assigned voxels in three layers (deeper, middle, and superficial) using the equi-volume approach (Kemper et al., 2018; Waehnert et al., 2014) as implemented in BrainVoyager (Brain Innovation, Maastricht, The Netherlands). This approach has been shown to reduce misclassification of voxels to layers, in particular for ROIs presenting high curvature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to methodological studies.

claim: Due to limitations in the UHF imaging resolution, MRI-defined layers indicate distance from the grey matter/white matter and the grey matter/cerebrospinal fluid boundaries rather than one-to-one mapping to the cyto-architectonically defined layers of the human neocortex.
source: Note that due to limitations in the UHF imaging resolution these MRI-defined layers indicate distance (i.e. cortical depth) from the grey matter/white matter and the grey matter/cerebrospinal fluid boundaries rather than one-to-one mapping to the cyto-architectonically defined layers of the human neocortex.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the imaging method.

claim: Participant responses showed a perceptual bias, that is, a significant shift in the perceived orientation of the test stimulus for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(11)=3.197, p=0.0085).
source: Participant responses showed a perceptual bias, that is, a significant shift in the perceived orientation of the test stimulus for adaptation compared to non-adaptation (t(11)=3.197, p=0.0085).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral experiment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Correlations between GE-EPI and 3D GRASE fMRI adaptation index were stronger for superficial (r = 0.465, p=0.019) and middle (r = 0.467, p=0.019) than deeper (r = 0.315, p=0.125) layers.
source: Correlations were stronger for superficial (r = 0.465, p=0.019) and middle (r = 0.467, p=0.019) than deeper (r = 0.315, p=0.125) layers.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the comparison between imaging sequences shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correspondence of results across sequences suggests that the results showing stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial and middle than deeper layers could not be simply due to vasculature confounds.
source: This correspondence of results across sequences suggests that our results showing stronger fMRI adaptation in superficial and middle than deeper layers could not be simply due to vasculature confounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison between imaging sequences.
